docs.D01_business_overview.md:
Title: A branded fee platform after the property and timeshare separations
Source: compiled from: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1585689/000158568918000030/a2017-q4earningsrelease.htm; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1585689/000158568918000120/a2018-q2earningsrelease.htm
Date: 2018-07-25

Hilton operates a global hotel brand, management and franchise system. Its July release describes more than 5,400 properties, nearly 880,000 rooms and operations in 106 countries and territories. The portfolio comprises 14 brands, including Hilton, Hampton, DoubleTree, Embassy Suites, Hilton Garden Inn and extended-stay offerings.

On January 3, 2017, Hilton separated Park Hotels & Resorts and Hilton Grand Vacations. The remaining public company is more focused on management and franchise fees, although some owned and leased hotel operations remain. It should not be analyzed as though it still owns the entire pre-separation property portfolio.

Third-party hotel owners provide much of the real-estate capital. Hilton supplies brands, reservations, distribution, operating standards and loyalty infrastructure, receiving franchise and management fees. New affiliated rooms can add fee revenue without requiring Hilton to fund the underlying hotel's full construction cost.

The network supports both sides of the platform. Owners seek occupancy, rates and guest acquisition; guests seek reliable brands, locations and recognition through Hilton Honors. Direct booking benefits include member discounts, Wi-Fi and points/money combinations. The value depends on actual owner economics and consumer preference, not simply the size of the membership database.

In Q2, franchise fees were $404 million, base/other management fees $84 million and incentive management fees $59 million. Owned/leased hotel revenue was $392 million, with $352 million associated operating expense. These lines show why fee growth is economically different from growth in property revenue.

CEO Christopher Nassetta reports that RevPAR growth and net-unit additions drove Q2 adjusted EBITDA growth of 10%. Development is a central reinvestment channel: the pipeline comprised 362,000 rooms, over half outside the US and over half under construction.

The model is asset-light, not demand-insensitive. Travel declines reduce fees, incentive fees can be especially cyclical, and financially stressed owners can defer construction or investment. Hilton also carries meaningful debt.

Evaluating durability therefore requires separate judgments about brand/loyalty advantages, the conversion of signed projects to operating rooms, normalized travel demand and disciplined capital returns. The economics are not those of a hotel REIT, and property ownership peers should not set the valuation without adjustment.
docs.D02_financial_snapshot.md:
Title: Financial record with explicit separation and accounting discontinuities
Source: compiled from: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1585689/000158568918000030/a2017-q4earningsrelease.htm; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1585689/000158568918000120/a2018-q2earningsrelease.htm
Date: 2018-07-25

Amounts are millions except EPS. Hilton's February release gives effect to January 2017 separations; it also includes pro-forma presentations for 2016. The July release retrospectively applies new revenue and pension accounting to its comparative periods. These are not interchangeable historical bases.

| Metric | 2016 pro forma, February basis | 2017, February basis | H1 2018, July basis |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Total revenue | 8,738 | 9,140 | 4,365 |
| Adjusted EBITDA | 1,763 | 1,965 | 1,000 |
| Diluted EPS | 0.36 | 3.85 | 1.21 |

FY2017 adjusted EBITDA grew 11% on the February pro-forma comparison. FY2017 EPS includes the provisional impact of tax reform and is not a clean forward earnings base. A comparable 2015 post-spin series was not recovered; mixing old consolidated Hilton into this table would create false precision.

On the July accounting basis, H1 2017 revenue was $3,972 million, operating income $541 million, net income $199 million and adjusted EBITDA $914 million. H1 2018 figures were $4,365 million, $685 million, $380 million and $1,000 million respectively.

Q2 2018 total revenue was $2,291 million and operating income $406 million. Total revenue includes $1,330 million of other revenues from managed/franchised properties, with $1,327 million related expenses. Their near-pass-through nature makes consolidated revenue margin a poor measure of the underlying fee business.

June long-term debt was $7.7 billion before financing costs/discount. Excluding capital leases and consolidated variable-interest-entity debt, the figure was $7.4 billion. Cash including restricted balances was $505 million, of which $82 million was restricted.

Management guides 2018 adjusted EBITDA to $2.070-$2.100 billion, adjusted EPS $2.64-$2.71, capital expenditures/contract acquisition costs excluding owner reimbursements $175-$200 million, and cash available for capital return $1.8-$1.9 billion.

That last measure is a company-defined capital-return projection, not a verified conventional CFO-minus-capex figure. A complete historical CFO/capex/FCF/ROIC series was not recovered. The available data support capital-light economics but do not justify labeling all fee revenue as free cash flow or ignoring debt-funded repurchases.
docs.D03_latest_results.md:
Title: Latest available earnings — room growth, fee growth and buybacks
Source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1585689/000158568918000120/a2018-q2earningsrelease.htm
Date: 2018-07-25

Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $555 million, up 10% and above the company's guidance range. Net income was $217 million, up 44%; diluted EPS was $0.71, and EPS adjusted for special items $0.70. The comparative adjusted EPS was $0.51.

Currency-neutral system-wide comparable RevPAR grew 4.0%, with the US up 3.5% and international markets up 5.9%. Both occupancy and average daily rate contributed. First-half RevPAR growth was 3.9%.

Management/franchise fee revenue grew 11% in Q2 and 12% in the first half. The release attributes growth to comparable RevPAR, increased license fees and new properties. This is important because the company's growth mechanism is not confined to same-hotel pricing or occupancy.

Hilton opened 123 hotels totaling 17,100 rooms in Q2. Net additions were 15,800 rooms, up 18% from the prior-year quarter. Management projects approximately 6.5% net-unit growth for the year.

The development pipeline reached 362,000 rooms in more than 2,370 hotels across 105 countries/territories. Approximately 186,000 rooms were under construction and 194,000 outside the US. A pipeline is not equivalent to an immediately earning asset, and not every signed project is assured to open on its original schedule.

Nassetta says: “This growth coupled with continued net unit growth resulted in Adjusted EBITDA growth of 10 percent, exceeding our expectations.” The source connects operating performance to both demand and distribution-system expansion.

Hilton repurchased 18.5 million shares in Q2 for approximately $1.3 billion, at an average $72.01, including shares from HNA and Blackstone exits. It returned nearly $1.6 billion through July in buybacks and dividends. The quarter's dividend was $0.15 a share.

Capital returns must be read alongside financing: April's $1.5 billion 5.125% notes helped fund the HNA repurchase and term-debt repayment. Repurchases are not all funded by current-period free cash flow.

The July outlook calls for full-year RevPAR growth of 3%-4%, fee revenue growth of 9%-11% and adjusted EBITDA growth of 8%-10%. October 24 results had not occurred at the October 15 cutoff and are excluded.
docs.D04_price_valuation.md:
Title: Price evidence and the correct earnings denominator
Source: compiled from: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1585689/000158568918000120/a2018-q2earningsrelease.htm; https://www.hotelnewsresource.com/article102020.html; https://fiscal.ai/company/NYSE_HLT/
Date: 2018-10-15

Historical daily data show an October 15 open of $73.34, close of $72.99 and volume of 2,994,000 shares. Only the historical row is used from the modern database. A verified cutoff 52-week range was not recovered.

The primary July release provides an authentic transaction benchmark: Hilton bought 18.5 million shares during Q2 at an average $72.01 per share. This includes large blocks connected with HNA's and Blackstone's exits and is not necessarily representative of a freely executable October price.

Using the cutoff close against the July adjusted FY2018 EPS guidance midpoint of $2.675 gives 27.3x. This uses the company's fiscal-year guidance, not next-year consensus. GAAP EPS guidance midpoint of $2.645 would imply 27.6x. The earlier repurchase benchmark would imply 26.9x on adjusted guidance.

The result shows why a broad claim of “about 20x forward earnings” requires a specified future earnings year and a documented forecast. No independently verified 2019 consensus EPS or forward multiple was recovered by the cutoff. The pack does not equate a later entry presentation's forward P/E with the company's contemporaneous 2018 guidance.

June cash including restricted funds was $505 million versus long-term debt of $7.7 billion. A simple debt-minus-cash measure is approximately $7.2 billion before distinguishing restricted cash, leases and variable-interest entities. These obligations matter even though the franchise business requires relatively little property capital.

A standard enterprise-value calculation also needs current outstanding shares. Q2 weighted diluted shares of 303 million are an earnings denominator, not a verified October spot count. Exact market capitalization and EV are therefore unavailable, not guessed, even with the historical closing quote now established.

The October 9 Baird/STR report says the hotel stock index rose 1.5% in September and was up 1.1% year to date; the brand sub-index rose 3.4% in September. This supports a mixed sector-sentiment account rather than a blanket claim that all hotel stocks had collapsed.

A valuation should bridge fee growth, unit expansion, capital requirements, leverage and cash returns. Historical GAAP EPS distorted by tax reform, pass-through revenue and property-REIT multiples are all weak shortcuts. The economic attraction can be real without establishing that any particular price meets the investor's return hurdle.
docs.D05_market_concerns.md:
Title: Cycle concerns against current industry demand evidence
Source: compiled from: https://seekingalpha.com/article/4208364-hotel-reits-another-record-year-for-hotel-demand; https://www.hotelnewsresource.com/article102020.html; https://www.hotelnewsresource.com/article102059.html
Date: 2018-10-11

The September 26 Hoya Capital industry review reports record hotel demand and more than 100 consecutive months of RevPAR growth. Its concern is supply growth, particularly in business-travel and urban markets, rather than an already established collapse in travel.

The article also distinguishes a strong 2018 corporate/luxury travel environment from the economics of hotel ownership. Owning hotels remains capital intensive; a favorable demand cycle does not eliminate renovation, labor or building costs. That distinction is essential when applying the commentary to a brand/fee company.

The October 9 Baird/STR stock-index report says investor expectations had become better aligned after second-quarter results and attention was shifting to 2019. Baird's Michael Bellisario points to continued modest RevPAR growth and stronger economic data. STR's Amanda Hite notes hurricane-affected comparisons but a forecast of further growth through 2019.

These sources do not support an unqualified claim that recession was certain or that current industry fundamentals were already poor. They establish a long expansion, supply concerns and the need to assess prospective rather than trailing demand.

The October 11 weekly STR report adds nuance. For the week ended October 6, US occupancy fell 0.9% to 70.9%; average daily rate rose 2.4% to $134.03; RevPAR rose 1.5% to $95.05. Houston had a steep decline against hurricane-boosted prior-year comparisons. A single week is not a normalized nationwide forecast.

The bear case for Hilton is that the combination of a mature travel cycle, new supply and leverage can constrain fee growth and capital returns. Pipeline openings depend on third-party owners and financing, so signed rooms do not fully insulate earnings from a downturn.

The favorable counterargument is that Hilton adds fee-paying units without funding all the physical real estate and benefits from a broad brand/loyalty network. Even that model remains exposed to occupancy/rates, owner health and incentive-management fees.

The key distinction is cyclical volatility versus impairment of the platform's long-run owner and guest value. None of these pre-cutoff articles establishes the answer through later events. They provide contemporaneous evidence to stress-test growth, not a license to assume either endless expansion or a predetermined recession.
docs.D06_peer_industry.md:
Title: Hilton and Marriott operating benchmarks
Source: compiled from: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1585689/000158568918000120/a2018-q2earningsrelease.htm; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1048286/000162828018010559/mar-2018q2earningsreleasee.htm; https://www.hotelnewsresource.com/article102059.html
Date: 2018-10-11

Marriott's August 6 second-quarter release provides a contemporaneous fee-platform comparison, rather than a hotel-property REIT. Its reported net income was $610 million, up 25% from $489 million, and adjusted net income $619 million, up 46%. Adjusted EBITDA was $939 million, up 15%.

Hilton's July 25 Q2 release reports $555 million adjusted EBITDA, up 10%, and $217 million net income, up 44%. Adjusted diluted EPS grew 37% to $0.70; system-wide comparable RevPAR grew 4.0%.

| Measure | Hilton Q2 2018 | Marriott Q2 2018 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Adjusted EBITDA | $555m | $939m |
| Adjusted EBITDA growth | 10% | 15% |
| Reported net income | $217m | $610m |
| Reported net-income growth | 44% | 25% |

The EBITDA figures are company-defined non-GAAP measures. Different brand mix, geography, accounting, integration costs and capital structures can materially affect comparability. Higher absolute EBITDA does not by itself establish superior unit economics or a cheaper valuation.

Hilton's fee lines grew 11% in the quarter and it guided approximately 6.5% annual net-unit growth. This illustrates the separate contribution of expanding the affiliated room base alongside same-property performance. The available peer extracts do not provide a sufficiently complete identical-basis fee/margin table to rank competitive moats numerically.

The October weekly STR data are a demand indicator, not directly comparable quarterly corporate results: US RevPAR rose 1.5% while occupancy fell 0.9%. They show that a rate-led revenue increase can coexist with weaker occupancy, and hurricane comparisons can distort regional year-over-year statistics.

Timestamped valuation ratios and complete financial tables for Hyatt and Wyndham were not recovered. No two-to-four-peer forward-multiple ranking is fabricated. The concrete comparison is to Marriott and to observed industry demand; full relative valuation remains a known gap.

When comparing these businesses, isolate management/franchise fees, pass-through revenue, owned/leased hotel exposure, owner-funded capex and debt. A property company and a branded distribution/loyalty system may share a travel cycle while having very different reinvestment needs and incremental returns on additional rooms.
docs.D07_pershing_context.md:
Title: Portfolio context before any public Hilton announcement
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/media/2014/09/02164905/Performance-Report-June-2018-PSH.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/10/07155009/2018-Interim-Financial-Statement-Letter-Only.pdf
Date: 2018-08-09

The July 2 performance report gives PSH June 30 AUM of $4,114.9 million. This is the listed vehicle, not total manager-wide AUM and not wholly undeployed cash. Reported net portfolio exposure was 113%, with no short exposure in the table.

The August 9 interim letter describes a portfolio of long-term stakes in “large capitalization, simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative, high-quality, dominant companies with catalysts for shareholder value creation.” It says the manager often acts as a catalyst through influential ownership and sometimes board representation.

The letter discusses newly disclosed investments in United Technologies and Lowe's. United Technologies offers separable aerospace, elevator and climate/control businesses with materially different capital needs and investor constituencies. Lowe's is presented as an operating-gap opportunity relative to Home Depot, with incoming CEO Marvin Ellison.

Other public discussions include ADP, Chipotle and the government-sponsored mortgage enterprises. First-half gross performance contributions included Chipotle +5.6 percentage points and ADP +5.1; Herbalife detracted 3.3 and Fannie/Freddie 3.3 combined. These are performance attributions, not position weights.

PSH returned 6.7% net through June and 12.7% through August 7. Its May $300 million own-share tender and subsequent insider purchases reflect capital allocation at the fund level. Those amounts should not be confused with cash available to buy a new operating-company stake.

The same interim letter describes Chipotle's early operational and digital improvement under Brian Niccol, illustrating that some portfolio companies require active business repair. A hotel fee platform with an established operating team could present a different kind of opportunity: continued execution and capital returns rather than replacing a broken core model.

Name-by-name current NAV weights, precise October fund cash and manager-wide AUM were not recovered in this pack. The analyst should avoid using stale attribution as a substitute for portfolio capacity.

No October 25 public announcement, later annual letter or later investor cost/return chart is supplied in the model-facing documents. Even though the assigned cutoff falls after a retrospectively identified first purchase, the pack is framed as an independent new-investment evaluation. The question is whether the platform, runway and price justify concentrated ownership on information already public.

drivers.driver: Asset-light, high-margin franchise and management-fee economics.
Brands, loyalty and distribution attract owners and guests.
Net-unit growth and development pipeline support long-duration compounding.
Chris Nassetta's team and disciplined cash returns.

answer_key.pack_quality_notes: Seven documents. Cutoff close $72.99/volume recovered. Three-year comparable post-spin history, historical FCF/ROIC, full peer valuations/current fund weights unavailable; explicit missingness. Strong pre-cutoff operating data and three dated industry reports; does not falsely claim universal hotel selloff.

valuation.eps_path: 8-10% EBITDA growth and 6.5% net unit growth compounded by share repurchases
valuation.downside_case: Cyclical recession leads to stagnant RevPAR and reduced development, limiting multiple expansion but preserving long-term asset-light margins.

drivers.driver: A high-quality, asset-light global hotel franchise platform generating recurring, high-margin royalty-like fees with minimal maintenance capex [D01], [D02].
Management’s disciplined execution of a capital-light strategy that prioritizes significant free cash flow return to shareholders, including $1.3 billion in Q2 2018 share repurchases [D03].
A durable growth runway supported by a global pipeline and ~6.5% net unit growth guidance, providing visibility into mid-teens EPS compounding [D03].
The market’s cyclical fear of a maturing travel cycle creates an attractive entry point for a dominant compounder currently trading at an adequate valuation [D05].

kill_criteria: Management shifts from an asset-light, fee-generative model toward capital-intensive hotel ownership.
Net-unit growth turns negative for two consecutive quarters, signaling brand decay or loss of competitive advantage with third-party developers.
A sustained decline in RevPAR combined with rising debt levels causes management to pause the share repurchase program.
A major shift in travel industry dynamics permanently alters the value proposition of loyalty programs and distribution infrastructure.
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A fundamental breakdown in the asset-light business model, such as a loss of franchise fee margin or a consistent failure to achieve net unit growth targets, would invalidate our thesis.
final.memo:
Hilton is a premier global hotel brand, management, and franchise platform that perfectly aligns with our standard for a simple, predictable, and free-cash-flow-generative business [D01]. By leveraging its 14 brands and massive loyalty infrastructure, the company operates an asset-light model that earns high-margin franchise and management fees while shifting real-estate capital requirements to third-party owners [D01].

The market has currently mispriced the company by focusing too heavily on a maturing travel cycle and potential near-term supply growth in urban markets [D05]. We believe these concerns are temporary and cyclical, obscuring the underlying strength of a business that grew fee revenue by 11% in Q2 2018 [D03].

We are able to acquire our stake at approximately 26.9x 2018 earnings, a reasonable price for a high-quality compounder with an 8-10% EBITDA growth algorithm [D03], [D04]. With ~6.5% annual net unit growth and aggressive, value-accretive share repurchases, we expect this position to generate a strong double-digit internal rate of return over our investment horizon [D03].

Our role is that of a long-term partner in a compounding-alone thesis, as the current leadership team is already effectively executing on the asset-light strategy [D01], [D03]. We will monitor the company's ability to maintain high margins through the economic cycle and its continued success in expanding its global footprint [D01], [D03].

While a severe global economic downturn remains the primary risk to RevPAR and the development pipeline, we are confident in the company's defensive characteristics and capital structure [D02], [D05]. Consequently, we are initiating a position at 4% of NAV with the intent to scale to 8% as we see continued operational success [D03].

valuation.eps_path: Mid-teens percentage growth driven by 6.5% net-unit growth and aggressive share buybacks
valuation.downside_case: RevPAR and incentive fee contraction during economic downturn

drivers.driver: A capital-light franchise model that generates high-margin, recurring royalty-like fees with minimal maintenance capex [D01].
Best-in-class net-unit growth of approximately 6.5% supported by a large, visible development pipeline of 362,000 rooms [D01, D03].
Management’s disciplined capital allocation, focusing on returning substantial excess free cash flow to shareholders via aggressive buybacks [D03].
The market misprices Hilton as a cyclical, leveraged hotel operator rather than a durable, high-quality compounder [D01, D05].

kill_criteria: Net-unit growth falls significantly below the 6-7% target for two consecutive quarters [D03].
Management shifts from an asset-light capital return strategy toward debt-fueled acquisitions of real estate assets [D01].
Hilton Honors loyalty program engagement metrics demonstrate material decline relative to peers [D01].
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A material, long-term degradation in the Hilton Honors loyalty ecosystem or a structural shift away from the asset-light franchise model toward capital-intensive real estate ownership would invalidate our investment thesis.
final.memo:
Hilton Worldwide is a premier global hospitality company operating an asset-light, high-margin franchise and management system [D01]. With a portfolio of 14 brands and nearly 880,000 rooms, Hilton maintains a significant competitive advantage through its global scale and the Hilton Honors loyalty platform, which drives consistent, recurring, royalty-like cash flows [D01].

The market currently misinterprets Hilton as a cyclical, high-leverage hotel operator, leading to valuation compression due to fears of a mature economic cycle [D05]. We believe this perspective ignores the structural transformation to a capital-light model that prioritizes fee generation over property ownership, insulating the company from the volatility of hotel real estate [D01].

We acquired our position at an implied 2018 P/E of approximately 26.9x [D04]. Given the company’s ability to grow earnings per share in the mid-teens through a combination of 6.5% net-unit growth and aggressive share repurchases, we anticipate a high rate of return as the market recognizes the durability and quality of Hilton's cash flows, leading to a re-rating of the multiple [D01, D03].

Our investment is supported by a robust pipeline of 362,000 rooms and management's proven commitment to returning capital to shareholders [D01, D03]. Under CEO Christopher Nassetta, the company has successfully optimized its balance sheet and structure to maximize long-term intrinsic value [D01, D03].

While a significant global macroeconomic downturn remains the primary risk, the asset-light business model provides a cushion against the operational and capital expenditures typically associated with hotel ownership [D01]. We will monitor net-unit growth and loyalty program metrics closely to ensure the long-term growth trajectory remains intact [D01, D03].

We are initiating a 10% position in Hilton, viewing it as a high-quality compounder that fits our mandate for simple, predictable, and dominant businesses [D01, D07].
